artists.biography:
Menswear (sometimes written "Menswe@r") were a Britpop band formed in October 1994 from Camden in London.

The beginnings of the band were a feature in a Select article about a supposed London mod revival led by Graham Coxon. Two individuals closely associated with the burgeoning Britpop scene, Chris Gentry and Johnny Dean, made references to a "top new unsigned band" (Menswear), an act which did not yet exist.

They later appeared on the cover of Melody Maker before they had released any material. Their dress sense was Mod (tight fitting suits etc.) whilst their music was influenced by both Blur's second album Modern Life Is Rubbish and Elastica. Gentry and Dean had a single song - called "Daydreamer" - but soon recruited friend Simon White, who contributed "I'll Manage Somehow" to add to the setlist necessary for their upcoming debut gig at a Britpop-oriented club on Regent Street called Smashing.

perplexity.description:
Menswear’s ¡Hay Tiempo! is the band’s second studio album, originally recorded in 1997 but not widely released until decades later. Musically, the album marks a significant departure from the Britpop sound of their debut, Nuisance, embracing a broader, more expansive sonic palette influenced by the US West Coast. The record blends elements of rock, pop, and country rock, featuring lush arrangements, widescreen melodies, and a more introspective songwriting approach. Produced by Chris Allison and mixed by Dave Bascombe, ¡Hay Tiempo! showcases a band evolving beyond their early mod-pop roots into a more mature and ambitious style.

In the context of Menswear’s discography, ¡Hay Tiempo! stands as a pivotal but long-unheard chapter. After the commercial and critical attention surrounding their debut, the band sought to distance themselves from the increasingly insular London music scene, resulting in an album that was both stylistically adventurous and commercially risky. Despite its ambition and the quality of its songwriting, shifting musical trends and internal band tensions led to the album being shelved after its completion. For years, it remained unreleased outside of Japan, earning a reputation as one of Britpop’s “lost” albums. When it finally received a wider release, it was met with critical acclaim for its bold evolution and its place as a unique artifact of late-1990s British rock.
